title: {{NAME}} and the Last Light of the Ember Herd
moral: The most powerful thing you can give someone is the belief that they are not alone.

pages.content:
The Ember Reaches were named for what happened there at dusk, when the whole landscape caught the last of the sun and burned, softly, in every shade of amber and copper and gold. The hills rolled and glowed. The grass was warm underfoot even after the light faded. And through the middle of it all ran a river that caught the last light like a long, slow flame.

{{NAME}} arrived at the boundary of the Ember Reaches by the specific method of jumping from the roof of a parking structure, which was the kind of decision you only made if you were reasonably sure a cape was going to do its job.

It did. He landed well.

He had been called here by a signal, a thin, high frequency that only certain people could perceive, though what qualified you to perceive it was something no one had ever adequately explained. It had woken him at three in the morning and led him, step by step, to the edge of this burning landscape.

Something in the valley below needed help. He could feel it in the same bone-deep way you felt the right answer before you found the words.

pages.content:
The last of the Ember Herd were three.

{{NAME}} found them in the valley beside the slow river, and the sight stopped him where he stood. They were unicorns, but unlike any he might have imagined in a calmer moment. They were the colour of living fire, coats shifting between orange and deep red-gold, their manes like slow flames, their horns dark iron with cores that glowed amber from within.

All three were lying down. Not resting. Something was wrong in a quieter, more serious way.

A hero named Solace was already there, kneeling beside the largest of the three, her own power a soft silver luminescence that she was pressing into the unicorn's side with both hands. She looked up at {{NAME}} with the expression of someone who had been working hard at a problem for hours.

"The Fade," she said. Not the weather phenomenon. Something older. The slow dimming that happened to magical creatures when the world forgot them, when no one believed in what they were anymore. "It's been accelerating. I can slow it." She shook her head. "I can't stop it alone."

pages.content:
{{NAME}} pressed both hands to the second unicorn, a smaller one whose coat had faded to the colour of ash at its edges. He pushed his power outward, not the flashy, visible kind, but the quieter one he'd been born with: the ability to make someone feel entirely, genuinely seen.

It worked differently on magical creatures than on people. Where people relaxed, unicorns blazed.

The second unicorn's coat kindled. Not fully, not yet, but a seam of fire-gold opened along its flank where his hands rested, spreading slowly inward like a coal catching air.

Solace saw it. "More," she said. "Don't stop."

They worked in tandem. Two heroes, two unicorns, Solace silver and steady and brilliant, {{NAME}} pouring the specific warmth of being witnessed into a creature that had been un-witnessed for too long.

The third unicorn, the smallest, raised its head.

Its eyes, which had been clouding, cleared. Its horn, dark and cold, began to glow amber from the base upward, slowly, the way dawn moves, each centimetre winning back the light. It made a sound, low and warm and precisely like hope given a voice.

Solace exhaled a breath she had been holding for hours.

pages.content:
The largest unicorn rose. Slowly, with the deliberate effort of something reclaiming itself.

When it was fully standing, it shook its mane, and the motion sent a cascade of fire-sparks drifting upward into the evening air, hanging like miniature stars, each one a perfect point of amber light. The second unicorn rose beside it. Then the third.

All three stood together at the edge of the slow river, fire-coats fully blazing, horns lit from base to tip in the warm dark gold of embers that have found their heat again. They were not fully healed. That would take longer, the steady rebuilding of the world's remembering. But they were present. They were bright.

The largest unicorn turned to {{NAME}} and regarded him with eyes that contained the full memory of fire. It touched its horn to the starburst on his chest, and the emblem blazed white for a moment, then resettled into its usual form, warmer and brighter than before.

{{NAME}} felt it in his chest: a warmth that moved inward rather than outward, filling rather than leaving.

"That means you're remembered too," Solace said quietly, watching. "That's what they give. What they have to give."

pages.content:
They stayed at the river until full dark, which in the Ember Reaches was not dark at all, because the three unicorns lit the whole valley with a steady, breathing amber glow.

Solace was good company. She had been a hero for nine years and had the particular quality of someone who had seen a great deal and was at peace with most of it. She told {{NAME}} about the Ember Herd's history in a voice as unhurried as the river beside them, while the three unicorns stood in the shallows and breathed fire-light into the water.

"They'll be all right now?" {{NAME}} asked.

"For a while," she said honestly. "They need people to know them. That's the whole of it. They need to be known."

{{NAME}} understood that, in ways that went deeper than unicorns.

He flew home slow and low, watching the Ember Reaches recede below, still glowing. His boots were warm on his feet when he set them by the door. He was in bed before the amber light of the valley had completely faded from his eyes.

He thought of the largest unicorn's eyes, which had held the full memory of fire.

And he found himself wondering, as sleep took him gently, what else in the world had been waiting, quietly, to be seen.
